blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this 1980 paper by Lehman as a foundational work that reframes software development as an ongoing evolutionary process rather than a one-time creation. The blog emphasizes Lehman's key insight that change is intrinsic to software systems, especially those interacting with the real world, and that maintenance costs dominate the software lifecycle. Colyer notes how the paper's observations remain strikingly relevant today, suggesting that software evolution problems may persist for decades. The post praises Lehman's classification of programs into S-programs (formally specifiable), P-programs (real-world problem solutions), and E-programs (embedded societal activities), and underscores the limitations of formal methods for the latter two classes where correctness depends on real-world outcomes rather than formal specifications.
paper_title: Programs, life cycles, and laws of software evolution
